title: Measuring What a Mind Detects
endLine: Fixed rules and controls separate sensory signals from noise and bias.

scenes.tts: How can you measure what another mind detects? A baby cannot speak, and a person's report shifts with expectation. Every sense also carries random fluctuation on every trial. Psychophysics turns controlled trials into precise measures of perception.
scenes.caption: How can you measure what another mind detects? A baby cannot speak, and a person's report shifts with expectation. Every sense also carries random fluctuation on every trial. Psychophysics turns controlled trials into precise measures of perception.
scenes.visual: Establish one carried world (schematic) filling the frame: the Psychophysics Bench, with three connected zones left to right. Left: a glowing stimulus dial pulsing gently. Centre: a shimmering response wave fluctuating randomly up and down. Right: a subject silhouette facing a choice icon with a bright question mark appearing first, before the narrator speaks. On 'baby cannot speak', the silhouette briefly morphs into an infant; on 'shifts with expectation', a sliding criterion bar drifts right and left; on 'controlled trials', the bench locks into crisp calibrated tick marks while ambient noise keeps drifting.
scenes.narration: How can you measure what another mind detects? A baby cannot speak, and a person's report shifts with expectation. Every sense also carries random fluctuation on every trial. Psychophysics turns controlled trials into precise measures of perception.

scenes.visual: Keep the carried Psychophysics Bench active with gentle ambient drift on the centre noise wave (schematic). Bold high-contrast title 'Measuring What a Mind Detects' fades in over the upper bench, holds cleanly, then fades out.

scenes.tts: Start by holding one response rule fixed across repeated trials. A detection threshold is the smallest stimulus a person reports detecting. A rat cannot speak, so labs measure a stand-in. Calibrated von Frey filaments of rising stiffness give a withdrawal threshold. Many labs use the force that lifts a paw half the time.
scenes.caption: Start by holding one response rule fixed across repeated trials. A detection threshold is the smallest stimulus a person reports detecting. A rat cannot speak, so labs measure a stand-in. Calibrated von Frey filaments of rising stiffness give a withdrawal threshold. Many labs use the force that lifts a paw half the time.
scenes.visual: On the carried bench (schematic): lock the right-side response rule icon with a steady highlight, then step the left stimulus dial upward across repeated trials. A response curve rises from low to high on the right readout; a glowing marker settles at the smallest stimulus reported and gets labelled 'Detection threshold'. Then the left stimulus morphs into calibrated von Frey filaments of increasing stiffness touching a rodent paw icon; the readout settles at the force that lifts the paw half the time, labelled 'Withdrawal threshold'.
scenes.narration: Start by holding one response rule fixed across repeated trials. A detection threshold is the smallest stimulus a person reports detecting. A rat cannot speak, so labs measure a stand-in. Calibrated von Frey filaments of rising stiffness give a withdrawal threshold. Many labs use the force that lifts a paw half the time.

scenes.tts: To test a baby's sight, use forced-choice preferential looking. Infants prefer a pattern to a plain field. A striped grating appears beside a gray field of equal brightness. An observer who cannot see which side holds the stripes judges the gaze. The finest grating reliably looked at gives acuity.
scenes.caption: To test a baby's sight, use forced-choice preferential looking. Infants prefer a pattern to a plain field. A striped grating appears beside a gray field of equal brightness. An observer who cannot see which side holds the stripes judges the gaze. The finest grating reliably looked at gives acuity.
scenes.visual: Transform the left stimulus stage of the carried bench into two side-by-side panels of equal luminance (schematic): one striped grating, one plain gray field. An infant silhouette in the centre turns its gaze arrow toward the striped panel before the narrator names the preference. A screen blocks the panels from a right-side observer icon, who scores left or right purely from the infant's gaze. The stripes narrow smoothly across trials until the gaze stops favouring the grating; the finest grating reliably followed marks 'Acuity'.
scenes.narration: To test a baby's sight, use forced-choice preferential looking. Infants prefer a pattern to a plain field. A striped grating appears beside a gray field of equal brightness. An observer who cannot see which side holds the stripes judges the gaze. The finest grating reliably looked at gives acuity.

scenes.tts: Why is there always a faintest detectable stimulus? On each trial, responses fluctuate around their mean, with a spread measured as a standard deviation, S D. Detectability, d prime, is the shift in mean response a signal causes, divided by that noise S D. Psychophysics pairs controlled stimuli with fixed rules to separate signals from noise and bias.
scenes.caption: Why is there always a faintest detectable stimulus? On each trial, responses fluctuate around their mean, with a spread measured as a standard deviation, SD. Detectability, d′, is the shift in mean response a signal causes, divided by that noise SD. Psychophysics pairs controlled stimuli with fixed rules to separate signals from noise and bias.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the centre response axis of the carried bench (schematic). A baseline bell curve of noisy trials shimmers gently; a horizontal double arrow marks its width, labelled 'Noise SD', right before the narrator names it. A stimulus pulses on the left, sliding a second bell curve rightward; a bracket spans the distance between the two peaks, labelled 'Mean shift'. Above the curves, the formula builds as spoken: 'd′ = Mean shift / Noise SD'. On the final sentence, the full three-zone bench pulls back into view with crisp labels 'Controlled stimulus', 'Signal vs noise', and 'Fixed rules'.
scenes.narration: Why is there always a faintest detectable stimulus? On each trial, responses fluctuate around their mean, with a spread measured as a standard deviation, SD. Detectability, d′, is the shift in mean response a signal causes, divided by that noise SD. Psychophysics pairs controlled stimuli with fixed rules to separate signals from noise and bias.

scenes.tts: Now test your intuition. In twenty fourteen, Puts and colleagues measured static finger-vibration thresholds in autistic and typically developing children. The autistic cohort averaged nine point one three micrometres, against six point five nine. Does that higher threshold show better or poorer detection?
scenes.caption: Now test your intuition. In 2014, Puts and colleagues measured static finger-vibration thresholds in autistic and typically developing children. The autistic cohort averaged 9.13 micrometres, against 6.59. Does that higher threshold show better or poorer detection?
scenes.visual: On the carried bench, the left stimulus dial becomes a vibrating probe touching a fingertip outline (schematic). On the right readout, two clean vertical bars grow to heights computed directly from the data: 6.59 µm (typically developing, n = 67) and 9.13 µm (autistic, n = 32; ages 8 to 12; Puts and colleagues, 2014). As the narrator asks the question, a high-contrast question banner appears across the top: 'Higher threshold: better or poorer detection?'
scenes.narration: Now test your intuition. In 2014, Puts and colleagues measured static finger-vibration thresholds in autistic and typically developing children. The autistic cohort averaged 9.13 micrometres, against 6.59. Does that higher threshold show better or poorer detection?

scenes.visual: Hold the two computed threshold bars (6.59 µm and 9.13 µm) and the question banner 'Higher threshold: better or poorer detection?' on the bench while a smooth countdown ring sweeps continuously through the pause.

scenes.tts: Poorer detection. A higher threshold sounds better, yet the stimulus had to grow larger before it was reported. Subtract six point five nine from nine point one three: two point five four micrometres. Divided by six point five nine, that is thirty eight point five per cent higher.
scenes.caption: Poorer detection. A higher threshold sounds better, yet the stimulus had to grow larger before it was reported. Subtract 6.59 from 9.13: 2.54 micrometres. Divided by 6.59, that is 38.5 per cent higher.
scenes.visual: The banner resolves to 'Poorer detection' as the left fingertip vibration amplitude visibly grows wider to reach the taller 9.13 µm bar (bar heights and equations computed from the given numbers). Next to the bars, each arithmetic step appears exactly as spoken: '9.13 − 6.59 = 2.54 µm', then a bracket spans the gap between the bars, then '2.54 / 6.59 = 38.5% higher'.
scenes.narration: Poorer detection. A higher threshold sounds better, yet the stimulus had to grow larger before it was reported. Subtract 6.59 from 9.13: 2.54 micrometres. Divided by 6.59, that is 38.5 per cent higher.

scenes.tts: Still, a threshold only answers what its task tests. Lab detection cannot measure everyday distress, and paw withdrawal is a reflex, not unpleasantness. Practice, repeated testing, expectation, and grader bias can also mislead. Guard against them with masked observers, masked grading, and randomized control groups.
scenes.caption: Still, a threshold only answers what its task tests. Lab detection cannot measure everyday distress, and paw withdrawal is a reflex, not unpleasantness. Practice, repeated testing, expectation, and grader bias can also mislead. Guard against them with masked observers, masked grading, and randomized control groups.
scenes.visual: Keep the carried bench (schematic). A clean divider separates the right-side lab threshold gauge from an 'Everyday distress' icon, and a brief paw-lift arrow splits away from an 'Unpleasantness' label to show distinct quantities. Then three drifting hazard tags ('Practice', 'Expectation', 'Grader bias') creep toward the readout and are swept aside by shield icons labelled 'Masked grading' and 'Randomized controls'.
scenes.narration: Still, a threshold only answers what its task tests. Lab detection cannot measure everyday distress, and paw withdrawal is a reflex, not unpleasantness. Practice, repeated testing, expectation, and grader bias can also mislead. Guard against them with masked observers, masked grading, and randomized control groups.

scenes.tts: Those safeguards unlocked discoveries. In nineteen forty two, Hecht, Shlaer and Pirenne measured the faintest flashes people could see. Those flashes gave so few absorptions, spread over about five hundred rods. They concluded one quantum of light, a single photon, is enough to excite a rod. Single toad-rod recordings showed it directly in nineteen seventy nine.
scenes.caption: Those safeguards unlocked discoveries. In 1942, Hecht, Shlaer and Pirenne measured the faintest flashes people could see. Those flashes gave so few absorptions, spread over about 500 rods. They concluded one quantum of light, a single photon, is enough to excite a rod. Single toad-rod recordings showed it directly in 1979.
scenes.visual: On the carried bench (schematic), the left stimulus becomes a dim flash of light landing on a dense grid representing about 500 rod cells; only a few scattered dots light up, highlighting a single rod firing a clear pulse, tagged 'Hecht, Shlaer & Pirenne, 1942'. On the final sentence, a small electrode trace confirms a single-quantum step on a toad rod, tagged 'Baylor, Lamb & Yau, 1979'.

scenes.tts: In twenty seventeen, Schvartz-Leyzac, Zwolan and Pfingst tested seven adults listening through an implanted electrode array. Going from twenty active electrodes to eight meant speech had to be louder against background noise. With the touch thresholds above, these results show what controlled trials can measure.
scenes.caption: In 2017, Schvartz-Leyzac, Zwolan and Pfingst tested seven adults listening through an implanted electrode array. Going from 20 active electrodes to 8 meant speech had to be louder against background noise. With the touch thresholds above, these results show what controlled trials can measure.
scenes.visual: On the carried bench (schematic), the left stimulus switches to a speech wave rising above background noise beside an implanted array of 20 lit electrode contacts. Contacts dim out from 20 down to 8 active; the speech wave must climb visibly higher above the noise floor to cross the readout threshold, tagged 'Schvartz-Leyzac, Zwolan & Pfingst, 2017'. On the final sentence, small icons for vision, touch, and hearing settle smoothly along the bench as the controlled stimulus, noise axis, and fixed-rule readout glow together.

scenes.visual: The carried bench softens into a calm background with subtle ambient drift on the noise wave (schematic), while the end-card rule appears centred in large high-contrast type: 'Fixed rules and controls separate sensory signals from noise and bias.'
